summary: Describes a compression method for TLS using a lossless algorithm, DEFLATE, in addition to the default of no compression. TLS can negotiate compression during the handshake and apply it in the record protocol. It was updated by RFC 8447 and RFC 8996.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 3749 defines DEFLATE as a compression method TLS peers can negotiate and use for record data. It also explains how TLS handles compression state and warns that compressed lengths can reveal information.

questions: how does tls deflate compression work
what is the deflate compression method in tls
what compression method values does tls reserve
what happens to compression state when a tls session resumes
subtitle: Adds a standardized DEFLATE compression method to TLS and defines identifier-allocation rules.

tldr.problem: TLS could negotiate compression, but its only standardized method meant no compression. Implementations lacked a shared compression method they could use interoperably.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 3749 assigns identifier 1 to stateful DEFLATE and divides the one-byte compression-method space into standards, specification-required and private-use ranges. It also defines behavior for compression history and session resumption.
tldr.outcome: TLS gained a standardized compression method, with cautions about data-length leakage and expansion. RFC 3749 has been updated by RFC 8447 and RFC 8996.

today: RFC 3749 is a Proposed Standard published in May 2004. It has been updated by RFC 8447 and RFC 8996, and it has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Why TLS Compression Needed a Standard
sections.content:
TLS can negotiate a lossless compression method during its handshake and apply that method in the record protocol. Before RFC 3749, TLS standardized only CompressionMethod.null, which sends record data without compression.

Compression can reduce bandwidth and latency when a connection carries large amounts of data. RFC 3749 defines an additional method for TLS; specifying the compressed data format and algorithm themselves is outside its scope.
sections.plainLanguage: TLS already had a place to negotiate compression but no shared method beyond no compression. This RFC defines one method so implementations can use the same choice.

sections.title: Compression Method Identifiers
sections.content:
The TLS CompressionMethod field is one byte and can identify up to 256 methods. RFC 3749 reserves values 0-63 for IETF Standards Track protocols, 64-223 for non-Standards Track methods and 224-255 for private use.

The existing null method keeps identifier 0. This RFC assigns identifier 1 to DEFLATE. IANA assigns identifiers from each range using its corresponding policy.
sections.plainLanguage: TLS identifies each compression method with a number. The RFC assigns a number to DEFLATE and reserves different number ranges for formal standards, other methods and private use.

sections.title: Stateful DEFLATE Compression
sections.content:
The DEFLATE compression method is described in RFC 1951. It is stateful: the compressor can maintain state across compressed records. RFC 3749 recommends that future standardized compression methods for TLS also be stateful.

DEFLATE lets the sender choose among settings with different compression ratios, processing speeds and memory needs. The receiver must adjust to the sender's selected settings. All submitted data must appear in compressed output; flushing ensures each packet payload can be decompressed completely.

A compression method that exceeds the expansion limits in the TLS specification must not be used with TLS.
sections.plainLanguage: DEFLATE can retain compression state across records. The receiver follows the sender's settings, and each output payload must contain enough data to be decompressed completely.

sections.title: History and Session Resumption
sections.content:
Compression history across packets can improve the compression ratio, but a packet may then contain information needed to decompress another packet. History therefore requires reliable delivery in sequence. TLS and its lower layers provide those properties, so a compression method may use history when it supports it.

TLS session resumption creates another connection using an existing session. On resumption, the compression algorithm must remain the same, but the compression state and history must be cleared. This avoids requiring other systems, such as load balancers, to preserve the old compression state.
sections.plainLanguage: A compression method may use earlier records to improve compression. When a TLS session resumes, it keeps the same method but clears the old compression history.

sections.title: IANA Assignment Policies
sections.content:
IANA maintains the TLS compression-method identifier registry. Values from 0-63 are assigned through Standards Action. Values from 64-223 use Specification Required, and values from 224-255 are for Private Use.

The registry includes DEFLATE's identifier and provides a defined path for later methods to receive identifiers without conflicting with the existing assignments.
sections.plainLanguage: IANA manages the list of TLS compression identifiers. The assignment process depends on which reserved range a method uses.

sections.title: Length Leakage and Expansion Risks
sections.content:
Compression combined with encryption can reveal information through length. Two inputs with the same original length may produce compressed data of different lengths, and an observer may infer information from those differences. Some TLS cipher suites conceal length less than others, so the RFC says to consider this risk when using compression.

Compression implementations are complex and can contain errors such as buffer overruns. Compressed input can also expand greatly when processed. The TLS rules require lossless compression, limit content-length increase to 1,024 bytes and limit total content length to 2^14 bytes.
sections.plainLanguage: Encrypted data length can still reveal information after compression. Implementations must also enforce the TLS expansion limits so compressed input cannot grow without bound.
